verses.text: Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jedidah the daughter of Adaiah of Bozkath.
He did that which was right in Yahweh’s eyes, and walked in all the way of David his father, and didn’t turn aside to the right hand or to the left.
In the eighteenth year of king Josiah, the king sent Shaphan, the son of Azaliah the son of Meshullam, the scribe, to Yahweh’s house, saying,
“Go up to Hilkiah the high priest, that he may count the money which is brought into Yahweh’s house, which the keepers of the threshold have gathered of the people.
Let them deliver it into the hand of the workmen who have the oversight of Yahweh’s house; and let them give it to the workmen who are in Yahweh’s house, to repair the damage to the house,
to the carpenters, and to the builders, and to the masons, and for buying timber and cut stone to repair the house.
However there was no accounting made with them of the money that was delivered into their hand; for they dealt faithfully.”
Hilkiah the high priest said to Shaphan the scribe, “I have found the book of the law in Yahweh’s house.” Hilkiah delivered the book to Shaphan, and he read it.

Shaphan the scribe came to the king, and brought the king word again, and said, “Your servants have emptied out the money that was found in the house, and have delivered it into the hands of the workmen who have the oversight of Yahweh’s house.”
Shaphan the scribe told the king, saying, “Hilkiah the priest has delivered a book to me.” Then Shaphan read it before the king.
When the king had heard the words of the book of the law, he tore his clothes.
The king commanded Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam the son of Shaphan, Achbor the son of Micaiah, Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah the king’s servant, saying,

“Go inquire of Yahweh for me, and for the people, and for all Judah, concerning the words of this book that is found; for great is Yahweh’s wrath that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not listened to the words of this book, to do according to all that which is written concerning us.”

So Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah, went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe (now she lived in Jerusalem in the second quarter); and they talked with her.
She said to them, “Yahweh the God of Israel says, ‘Tell the man who sent you to me,
“Yahweh says, ‘Behold, I will bring evil on this place, and on its inhabitants, even all the words of the book which the king of Judah has read.

Because they have forsaken me, and have burned incense to other gods, that they might provoke me to anger with all the work of their hands, therefore my wrath shall be kindled against this place, and it will not be quenched.’”
But to the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of Yahweh, tell him, “Yahweh the God of Israel says, ‘Concerning the words which you have heard,

because your heart was tender, and you humbled yourself before Yahweh, when you heard what I spoke against this place, and against its inhabitants, that they should become a desolation and a curse, and have torn your clothes, and wept before me; I also have heard you,’ says Yahweh.

‘Therefore behold, I will gather you to your fathers, and you will be gathered to your grave in peace. Your eyes will not see all the evil which I will bring on this place.’”’” So they brought this message back to the king.

footnotes.content: A boy-king at eight years old—Josiah came to the throne when most children are still learning their letters. Yet the Lord saw fit to put a tender heart in his small frame, and he grew into a man who would seek the Lord with all his might.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This is the posture the Lord treasures: a straight path, no turning aside. Josiah walked it. How often we are tempted left or right by the crowd's applause or the whisper of doubt—yet the narrow way remains the way of peace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In his eighteenth year, grown into manhood, Josiah sent Shaphan to the temple. It was an ordinary act of kingly duty—yet this small errand would change the nation's course, because a king willing to hear is already half-listening for what the Lord will say.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king's concern was practical: count the money, repair the house. His eye was on the temple's broken stones. He did not know that the greatest discovery lay in dusty shelves, waiting to be found.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A good king cares that the Lord's house be tended faithfully. The workmen knew their task: to restore what had fallen into disrepair. So it is with our own hearts—the Lord sends His Spirit to repair and rebuild what sin has cracked.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Timber, stone, the labor of hands—the physical work of repair cannot be rushed. So too with spiritual renewal; it requires both the work of the Lord's Spirit and the faithful hands of His people, each called to their task.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No accounting needed—they dealt faithfully. This small sentence speaks volumes: trustworthy people need no oversight. Honesty is its own accounting. Where trust is rooted in the fear of the Lord, oversight becomes unnecessary.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There it was: the book of the law, found where it had lain. How long had it sat silent? Yet the Lord knew exactly where His Word rested and the hour when a sincere heart would find it. Hilkiah received it and passed it on—faithful links in a chain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shaphan reported the ordinary business first: the money counted, the task assigned. Yet as his final word, he held back the greatest news. Sometimes the Lord's most powerful work arrives as an afterthought in our own telling of the day.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shaphan read the law aloud to the king. The words fell on ears that had never heard them—a nation that had drifted so far from God's Word that the book itself was a stranger. What a mercy that the Lord did not leave them without witness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He tore his clothes. That ancient gesture of mourning spoke what words could not—the king's shock at how far his people had wandered, his own complicity in their unfaithfulness. A tender heart recognizes its own need, and repentance begins with that rending.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Josiah gathered wise counselors—priest, officers, scribes, servants. A wise king knows he cannot discern the Lord's will alone. He calls the godly to his side and asks them, too, to hear what the Lord would say. Wisdom is always a circle, not a throne.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Great is Yahweh's wrath"—Josiah saw clearly that the book's words were not abstract; they were judgment spoken over his people. Yet in that very fear, he turned to inquire of the Lord. Terror of God is the beginning of wisdom, and it drove him toward, not away from, his God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Huldah the prophetess—a woman God chose to speak His Word in a moment when the king and priests needed to hear it. The Lord chooses His messengers not by their station but by their faithfulness. In the second quarter of the city, in ordinary clothes, she waited for this hour.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Huldah opened with what the Lord had to say, not what the king wished to hear. A true prophet's first loyalty is always to God's Word, not to comfort or royal favor. Yet even judgment contains the Lord's mercy—He speaks because He calls His people back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Evil on this place, on its inhabitants." The words were not soft. Yet the Lord does not judge without cause—each nation reaps what it has sown, and Judah had long since chosen her path. Even judgment is a witness to the gravity of God's covenant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The root lay plain: forsaken love, burned incense to other gods. A heart turned from the Lord does not fall silent—it speaks its rebellion louder and louder. Yet even here, the Lord's words come not in silence but in urgent, grieving witness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The prophet turns now to a different word—for the king. The Lord does not treat all alike. Josiah's own heart, his tears, his humility—these the Lord saw and honored. Repentance does not erase the nation's course, but it changes what the Lord will do with the repentant soul.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A tender heart, a humble spirit—readers today hear an echo in these words. How often does the Lord wait for a small turning, a moment when we simply stop and say, 'I was wrong'? Josiah did not know it would spare him from seeing the judgment he had inherited. He only knew to weep. The Lord saw.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gathered to his fathers in peace—the Lord promised Josiah rest before the storm. He would not live to see the fall of Jerusalem. A mercy granted not because the nation was spared, but because one man's heart was tender. The Lord never leaves His own without comfort, even in dark hours.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
